title: The Chapter on Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva's Perfect Penetration through Buddha-Recitation, with Commentary
author: Zhanran (commentary)
excerpt: Master Yinguang, in his Preface to the Re-issued Five Pure Land Scriptures, says: “Among the Mahāyāna scriptures, those that speak incidentally of the Pure Land are too numerous to count. But the chapter of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra on Mahasthamaprapta's Perfect Penetration through Buddha-Recitation is truly the most excellent instruction on Buddha-recitation. inline.s: Course
Textbook
Master Yinguang, in his Preface to the Re-issued Five Pure Land Scriptures, says:

“Among the Mahāyāna scriptures, those that speak of the Pure Land in passing are too numerous to number. Yet the chapter of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra on Mahasthamaprapta's Perfect Penetration through Buddha-Recitation is in truth the most excellent instruction on Buddha-recitation. If beings can truly recollect with ‘the six faculties gathered in, pure mindfulness in unbroken succession’, how could they fail to see the Buddha in the present and in the future — to realize at hand Perfect Penetration and, in the far future, accomplish the Buddha Way!”

[The Five Pure Land Scriptures] Beyond the Three Pure Land Scriptures, adding the Chapter on Samantabhadra's Vows and Conduct and the Chapter on Mahasthamaprapta's Perfect Penetration through Buddha-Recitation, together these are called the Five Pure Land Scriptures. [The Three Pure Land Scriptures] The three scriptures that the Pure Land School relies upon: the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life (the Larger Sūtra), the Sūtra on the Contemplation on the Buddha of Measureless Life (the Contemplation Sūtra), and the Amitābha Sūtra (the Smaller Sūtra).
Master Yinguang, in his Praise of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, says:
“Like a child who longs for his mother, so he longs for the World-Honored One
(Amitābha Buddha)

; and straightway he is shown grace. The cause-mind and the fruit-awakening are in perfect accord; at once he returns to the root and the source — the wonder of gathering in the six faculties can scarce be told.”
(Here “longing” carries the sense of remembrance.)

[Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva] This Bodhisattva, with the light of wisdom, universally illuminates all beings, freeing them from the three paths (the three evil destinies) and enabling them to gain supreme strength; moreover, when he walks, the entire ground of all the worlds in the ten directions trembles — hence he is called Mahasthamaprapta (Great Power Attained). Together with Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, he assists Amitābha Buddha in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; the world calls them the Three Holy Ones of the West. [The Three Paths] Also written as the three ways: the path of fire, the path of blades, and the path of blood — the same in meaning as the three evil destinies of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. First, the path of fire is the hell realm; because the beings suffering there are ever tormented by the heat of boiling cauldrons and burning coals, or because the fires there are so many, it is called the path of fire. Second, the path of blades is the hungry-ghost realm; because the beings there constantly suffer the torment of being driven by blades and staffs, it is called the path of blades. Third, the path of blood is the animal realm; because the beings suffering there — the strong subduing the weak — devour one another, drinking blood and eating flesh, it is called the path of blood. [Cause-mind] The mind in the causal stage; here it refers to beings' mind that recollects the Buddha. [Causal stage, fruit stage] From an ordinary being first arousing the mind to study the Buddha, up to the time before perfect Buddhahood is reached, this whole course is called the “causal stage”; reaching perfect Buddhahood is called the fruit stage. [Fruit-awakening] The awakening of the fruit stage; here it refers to the perfect great awakening of Amitābha Buddha.

The Chapter on Mahasthamaprapta's Perfect Penetration through Buddha-Recitation is one chapter of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra. At the Śūraṅgama assembly, the World-Honored One, at the request of Ānanda and the assembly, said to the great Bodhisattvas and the great Arhats who had exhausted their defilements:
“Now I ask you: when in the beginning you resolved your mind and awakened to the eighteen elements, who was perfect in Penetration
(who attained Perfect Penetration)
? Through what expedient means did you enter samādhi?”

[Exhaustion of defilements] The complete cutting off of all afflictions. “Defilement” is another name for affliction. [The eighteen elements] Combining the six sense faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; the six sense objects of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas; and the six consciousnesses of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind — these are called the “eighteen elements”. [Perfect Penetration] Pervading everything, fused and unobstructed. Here it refers to the principle of reality realized by the sublime wisdom of the sages. [Through what expedient means did you enter samādhi] By what means and method does one enter samādhi? [Samādhi] Also called samādhi (sān-mèi); it is the abiding of the mind in a single state without scattering.

Thereupon twenty-five great Bodhisattvas and great Arhats, each in turn, told of the gate by which they had attained Perfect Penetration. Among them, the last two — for ordinary practitioners the two most important gates — were Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva's gate of Buddha-Recitation Perfect Penetration and Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva's gate of ear-faculty Perfect Penetration. Then the World-Honored One said to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva: these twenty-five gates of Perfect Penetration
“are in truth without superiority or inferiority, without before or after. Now I wish to cause Ānanda to awaken: among these twenty-five methods of practice, which one suits his faculties?”

[Now I wish to cause Ānanda to awaken: among these twenty-five methods, which one suits his faculties] I now wish to cause Ānanda to awaken; of the twenty-five methods of practice, which one accords with his faculties and nature?
Mindful of Ānanda's fondness for extensive hearing, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva chose the gate of ear-faculty Perfect Penetration — the practice of “reversing the hearing to hear one's own nature”.

Yet the gate of ear-faculty Perfect Penetration suits only practitioners of sharp faculties, who realize their nature and cut off delusion. Now, in this age of the Dharma's decline, when desires are rampant and beings' faculties are mean and poor — for sentient beings, of these twenty-five methods of practice, which one suits their faculties? The answer is: Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva's gate of Buddha-Recitation Perfect Penetration. The World-Honored One, already three thousand years ago, taught in the Great Collection Sūtra:
Of the countless myriads who cultivate in the Dharma-ending age, scarce one attains the Way; only by relying on Buddha-recitation do they cross over birth-and-death.
Master Yinguang says:

“The Śūraṅgama Sūtra's chapter on Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva's Perfect Penetration through Buddha-Recitation is truly the most excellent instruction on Buddha-recitation. If beings can truly recollect with ‘the six faculties gathered in, pure mindfulness in unbroken succession’, how could they fail to ‘see the Buddha in the present and in the future’, to realize at hand Perfect Penetration and, in the far future, accomplish the Buddha Way!”
(Record of the Founding of the Great Hall of the Pure Land Practice Center on Mount Lingyan)
[Mahasthamaprapta, the Dharma Prince, together with his fifty-two companion Bodhisattvas, rose from their seats, bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet, and said to the Buddha:]

Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva and the fifty-two Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment, who had likewise come with him from the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, all rose at once from their seats, drew near before Śākyamuni Buddha, bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet, and with reverence Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva said to the Buddha:

[Mahasthamaprapta, the Dharma Prince] That is, Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva. Together with Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, he assists Amitābha Buddha in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; the world calls the three of them the Three Holy Ones of the West. According to the Sūtra on Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva Receiving the Prediction (Mahasthamaprapta is also named the Bodhisattva of Great Power Attained), after immeasurable, countless, inconceivable eons have passed, Amitābha Buddha will enter cessation, and Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva will then accomplish Buddhahood and fill his place, holding the power of transformation, bearing the title Tathāgata King of Mount of Universal Light and Merit; and after the Tathāgata King of Mount of Universal Light and Merit enters cessation, Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva will accomplish Buddhahood and fill his place, bearing the title Tathāgata King of Precious Mountain of Well-Dwelling Merit (also named Tathāgata King of Precious Mountain of Well-Dwelling Treasure). [Dharma Prince] An honorable title for great Bodhisattvas, because a great Bodhisattva is born into the house of the Dharma King (the Buddha) and is able to inherit and transmit the Dharma. [Of his own kind] Of the same rank, of the same class. Here it means that these fifty-two Bodhisattvas are the same as Mahasthamaprapta, all being Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment who came from the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. [Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment] The fifty-first of the fifty-two stages, the Bodhisattva about to realize the Buddha-fruit; his merit and wisdom are nearly equal to the Buddha's, hence he is called “Equal Enlightenment”. Also called the “Bodhisattva of One More Birth”, or the “Bodhisattva of the Vajra Mind”. For example, Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, and Maitreya Bodhisattva are all Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment.

[One more birth to fill the Buddha's place] Completing this single life, one is able to fill the position of the Buddha; this is another name for the Bodhisattva in the final body (the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment)
In the Amitābha Sūtra, the Buddha says:

“The beings born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are all avivartika (non-retrogressing); among them there are many in their last birth to fill the Buddha's place, and their number is so great that it cannot be known by reckoning, but can only be spoken of in terms of immeasurable, boundless asaṃkhyeyas.”

[The fifty-two stages] From an ordinary being to Buddhahood, a Bodhisattva in all passes through fifty-two stages: the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, Equal Enlightenment, and Wondrous Enlightenment. [Wondrous Enlightenment] Awakening oneself and awakening others, with awakening and practice perfectly fulfilled and wisdom and virtue inconceivable — this is called “Wondrous Enlightenment”; it is the supreme right awakening of the Buddha-fruit, and the one who realizes this right awakening is called a “Buddha”.
A questioner says: “The fifty-two Bodhisattvas are symbols of the fifty-two stages of Bodhisattvahood.”

Answer: This statement is not quite right. The fifty-two stages mean that a Bodhisattva, from an ordinary being to Buddhahood, in all passes through fifty-two stages, namely: the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, Equal Enlightenment, and Wondrous Enlightenment. Among these, Wondrous Enlightenment is the Buddha, not a Bodhisattva.

Question: Once beings are reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, they are free from birth-and-death and all attain Buddhahood in one lifetime. Why does it say here that only the Bodhisattva in his last birth can “fill the Buddha's place within this single life”?

Answer: There are two kinds of birth-and-death: compounded (sectional) birth-and-death and transmuted (transformational) birth-and-death. When it says “once beings are reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss they are free from birth-and-death and attain Buddhahood in one lifetime”, this “one lifetime” refers to one lifetime within compounded, sectional birth-and-death; whereas when it says “the Bodhisattva in his last birth fills the Buddha's place within this single life”, this “single life” refers to one lifetime within transmuted, transformational birth-and-death.

[Compounded (sectional) birth-and-death] For beings in the three realms and six destinies, because their lifespans are limited and their bodies have distinct sections, their birth-and-death is called “sectional birth-and-death”. One who has ended sectional birth-and-death has escaped the wheel and left the three realms. [Transmuted birth-and-death] The sages of the three vehicles (the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Bodhisattva vehicle), having already severed the delusions of views and thought and ended sectional birth-and-death, in the course of their practice find delusion ever ceasing and realization ever increasing; this transition of delusion and awakening differs from one period to the next, and the passage from an earlier period into a later one is like a single departure through birth-and-death — its transformation so subtle and inconceivable that it is called “transmuted birth-and-death”. One who ends transmuted birth-and-death perfectly realizes the Buddha-fruit.

[I recall that in the past, as many eons as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Immeasurable Light. In that eon twelve Tathāgatas appeared in succession. The last Buddha was named Beyond Sun and Moon Light; that Buddha taught me the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi.]

I recall that in the past, as many great eons as the sands of the Ganges ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Immeasurable Light. In the great eon in which He appeared, altogether twelve Tathāgatas appeared in the world in succession. The last of these Buddhas, named Beyond Sun and Moon Light, taught me to cultivate the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi.

[Sands of the Ganges] The Ganges is a great river of India; its waters carry much fine sand, and when the Buddha taught he often used the number of the sands of the Ganges to describe an exceedingly great number. [Buddha-Recitation Samādhi] The right concentration of Buddha-recitation, thoroughly seeing the original nature. Regarding the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi, see in detail
An Elucidation of Groping for the Elephant: Notes on the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi
In the following, Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva tells of the method by which the Buddha Beyond Sun and Moon Light taught him to cultivate the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi:

[It is as though there were two persons: one was altogether mindful, the other altogether forgetful. These two persons, were they to meet, would be as though they had not met; were they to see each other, it would be as though they had not seen.]

Suppose there are two persons, A and B. A devotes his whole mind to thinking of B, while B does not think of A in the least. Such two persons, even if they meet, might as well not have met; and even if they see each other, might as well not have seen.
[When the two are mindful of each other, and their mindfulness grows ever deeper, until, from life to life, they are like body and shadow, never apart or at variance.]

If both of these persons devoted their whole minds to thinking of each other, their mutual longing would grow ever deeper, engraved in heart and bone, so that, life after life, birth after birth, they would be inseparable as form and shadow, of one heart as one body, never turning from each other.
[From life to life] Life after life, birth after birth, in life and life, in birth and birth. [Like body and shadow] As inseparable as a body and its shadow.

[The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, in pity, bear beings in mind, as a mother thinks of her child. If the child flees away, of what use is her thinking, however deep? If the child thinks of the mother as the mother thinks of him, then mother and child, through life after life, are neither estranged nor far apart.]

The Buddhas of the ten directions, with love and compassion, bear beings in mind, just as a mother thinks of her son. If the son flees from his mother, though the mother longs for him, of what use is such earnest longing to him? If the son thinks of his mother as the mother thinks of him, then mother and son, through life after life, are neither estranged nor parted.

[Neither estranged nor far apart] The word “far” here carries the sense of “leaving”. That is, as said above: if both are entirely mindful of each other, their mutual longing grows ever deeper, engraved in heart and bone, so that, life after life, birth after birth, they are inseparable as form and shadow, of one heart as one body, never turning from each other.

The Buddhas, in pity, bear beings in mind as a mother thinks of her child; if the child (beings) thinks of the mother (the Buddha) as the mother thinks of him, then mother and child, through life after life, are neither estranged nor apart. Therefore, in one thought of recollecting the Buddha, in that one thought one receives the Buddha's reception and guidance; in thought after thought of recollecting the Buddha, in thought after thought one receives the Buddha's reception and guidance. Thus, in thought after thought recollecting the Buddha without forgetfulness, one is surely received and drawn to the Land of Bliss.
It should be specially noted: to recite the Buddha's name with the mouth while the mind thinks of other things is not recollecting the Buddha or reciting the Buddha.
The above similes set forth the principle of recollecting and reciting the Buddha; what follows sets forth the method of practice:

[If a being's mind recollects and recites the Buddha, then in the present and in the future he will surely see the Buddha, and be not far from Buddhahood. Without recourse to other expedient means, he will of himself open his mind. It is like a person steeped in incense whose body bears its fragrance. This is called “adorned with Fragrance and Light”.]

If a being's mind recollects and recites the Buddha, then in the present or in the future he will surely see the Buddha, and be not far from Buddhahood. He need not borrow any other gate; of himself he will make the mind clear and see the nature (of himself the mind opens). It is just like a person who has been steeped in incense: his body bears the fragrance. This is called “adorned with Fragrance and Light” — adorning oneself with the fragrance of virtue and the light of wisdom.

[Recollecting the Buddha] Thinking of the Buddha — as a wandering son thinks of his kind mother, so thinking of Amitābha Buddha. [Reciting the Buddha] Calling upon the name. [Recollecting and reciting the Buddha] Binding the mind upon the Buddha and calling upon the name. [In the present and in the future, surely will see the Buddha] In the present or in the future, surely one will see the Buddha. When the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi is accomplished, one can see the Buddha in the present (now). In the Instructions Pointing to the West, Bodhisattva Jueming Miaoxing says:
“If a person of great strength, with a single thought ever one and whole, attains the deep samādhi, he sees the Buddha now, in this very life.”
(See in detail
Instructions Pointing to the West (annotated)

) At the time of rebirth the Buddha comes to welcome and guide, which is seeing the Buddha in the future (to come). [Not far from Buddhahood] Not far from accomplishing Buddhahood, because having gone to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss one no longer revolves in samsara and never retrogresses, ever advancing upward, to attain Buddhahood in one lifetime — hence it is said to be not far from Buddhahood. [Without recourse to expedient means] One need not borrow any other gate. [Of himself the mind opens] Here “the mind opens” means seeing the Buddha of one's own nature, that is, the “seeing the nature” of the Chan (Zen) school. Master Ouyi, in his Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sūtra, says:

“Whether one holds on through practice-in-phenomena or through practice-in-principle, when one holds until the mind opens and one sees the Buddha of one's own nature, both are the unified mind of principle.”

Bodhisattva Jueming Miaoxing, in the Instructions Pointing to the West, concerning the incident of his past “when, single-mindedly and intently recollecting, he at once opened his mind and saw the Buddha in the present”, taught:
“In the past, in the time of Emperor Ming of the Jin, I received the body of a poor son. Because of this poverty and hardship, I made a great vow, saying: ‘Because of my
(through)
past karma
(the karmic offense of a former life)

, I receive this bitter retribution. If from this day I do not see Amitābha Buddha, am not born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and accomplish no merit, then even if I lose my body, I will never retreat or rest.’ Having made this vow, for seven days and seven nights, single-mindedly and intently I recollected, and at once my mind opened, and I saw the excellently marked, radiant light of Amitābha Buddha pervading the worlds of the ten directions. Before the Buddha I personally received the prediction; later, at the age of seventy-five, sitting at ease, I passed away, and was indeed born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

You should be of one intent and one mind, steadfastly cultivating this gate, and you will surely not be mistaken. If your resolve is once firmly set, you need not wait to be born in another life; even in this present life you will see the Buddha, just as I did in years past.
(See in detail
Instructions Pointing to the West (annotated)

) [Practice-in-phenomena and practice-in-principle] In upholding the Name and reciting the Buddha there are practice-in-phenomena and practice-in-principle. Practice-in-phenomena is recollecting Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; practice-in-principle is recollecting the Buddha of one's own nature. [Adorned with Fragrance and Light] When recollecting and reciting the Buddha is unbroken and pure mindfulness continues in succession, then the body (speech and action) bears the fragrance of virtue and the mind holds the light of wisdom; naturally one puts off the stench and escapes the darkness, evil deeds cease and idle thoughts subside, and one adorns oneself with the fragrance of virtue and the light of wisdom.
Question: How does one recollect and recite the Buddha?
Answer: Bind the mind upon the Buddha and call upon the name, thinking of Amitābha Buddha as a child thinks of his mother. The Sūtra on the Contemplation on the Buddha of Measureless Life says:

“The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, have the body of the Dharma-realm, entering into the minds of all beings. Therefore, when your minds think of the Buddha, that mind is itself the thirty-two marks and the eighty minor characteristics. That mind is making the Buddha; that mind is the Buddha. The ocean of the Rightly Fully Awakened Knowledge of all Buddhas is produced from the mind's thinking.”

[Body of the Dharma-realm] The body that pervades the Dharma-realm, that is, the Dharma-body, one of the three bodies of the Buddha. [The three bodies] The Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Response-body. The Dharma-body, also called the self-nature body or the Dharma-nature body, is the ever-abiding, never-ceasing true nature that everyone innately possesses; only we beings are deluded and do not manifest it, whereas the Buddha is awakened and has realized it. The Reward-body is formed of the Buddha's wisdom and merit, and is distinguished as the Reward-body enjoyed by oneself and the Reward-body enjoyed by others. The Reward-body enjoyed by oneself is the body in which the Buddha himself enjoys the Dharma-bliss of inner realization; the Reward-body enjoyed by others is the body that the Buddha manifests in order to teach the Bodhisattvas of the ten grounds. The Response-body, also called the response-transformation body or the transformation body, is the Buddha-body manifested in response to the opportunities of beings. [The thirty-two marks] The inner virtue of a Buddha or a wheel-turning sage king, displayed upon his body, amounts to thirty-two marks. [The eighty minor characteristics] The eighty kinds of excellent attributes that the Buddha's body possesses. [The ocean of the Rightly Fully Awakened Knowledge of all Buddhas] Buddhas as numerous as the water of the great ocean. “Rightly Fully Aware” is one of the Buddha's ten epithets; “the Rightly Fully Awakened of all Buddhas” means all the Buddhas. The word “ocean” is a metaphor for the abundance of their number, like the water of the great sea. [The ocean of the Rightly Fully Awakened Knowledge of all Buddhas is produced from the mind's thinking] The Buddhas, as numerous as the water of the great ocean, all become Buddhas by having the mind think of the Buddha. That is, as this scripture says:
“If a being's mind recollects and recites the Buddha, then in the present and in the future he will surely see the Buddha, being not far from Buddhahood
(not far from Buddhahood)

In the great affairs of life, none is greater than birth and death. Buddha-recitation is the foremost great matter aimed solely at freeing oneself from birth and death — how would one dare to lose it? Therefore, a single name of the Buddha — do not forget it; and if it happens to be forgotten, remember it and recite it again. At all times, through the six periods of the day and night, keep the great name firmly in mind; recite long, and it will grow familiar, until there is no thought that does not remember. Remember: let the mind be constantly mindful, never forgetting the Buddha!
Master Shandao says:
“Therefore the Great Sage
(Śākyamuni Buddha)

, out of pity, directly urges one to single-mindedly call the name. It is precisely because calling the name is easy that, with its continuation, rebirth is attained. If one can be mindful in thought after thought until the end of life, then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn. Why is this? Because, free of outward distractions and incidents, one has right mindfulness; because it accords with the Buddha's fundamental vows; because it violates no instruction; because it follows the Buddha's words. But if one abandons single-mindedness and cultivates mixed practices, of a hundred one will hardly find one or two, and of a thousand hardly three or four. Why is this? Because distractions and incidents stir wildly and right mindfulness is lost; because it does not accord with the Buddha's fundamental vows; because it violates the instruction; because it does not follow the Buddha's words; because mindfulness is not continuous; because the mind does not continuously think to repay the Buddha's grace; because, though one does the practices, the mind is ever turned toward fame and gain; because one delights in drawing near to distractions and incidents, hindering oneself and hindering others from the right practice of rebirth. In comparison I have seen
(commonly seen)
the monastics and laypeople of the various places
(clergy and laity)

: their understanding and practice differ, and their single-mindedness and mixed practice are not the same. But for those who single-mindedly practice, of ten, ten are reborn; for those who cultivate mixed practices without reaching the deep mind, of a thousand there is not one. I wish all people to think this over well: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, one must steel the mind and restrain oneself, day and night without ceasing, to the end of life. When the former thought ends in death, the latter thought is reborn, and for long ages and countless eons one enjoys the bliss of the unconditioned Dharma, and at last attains Buddhahood — how joyful is that!”
(Records of the Sages and Worthies of the Pure Land: Master Shandao of the Tang, the Second Patriarch of the Pure Land School)
The Repentance Master Ciyun says:
“Whenever, in public office
(in official duties)
or in private life
(in daily living)
, one passes through various circumstances and affairs; though hurried
(in haste)
, yet within, the mind never forgets the Buddha and recollects the Pure Land. It is like an ordinary person with a pressing matter
(an urgent matter)
held fast in mind; though he goes through conversation, coming and going, sitting and lying, and all manner of tasks, none of it hinders his secret recollection
(that is, it does not hinder the thought within the mind)

: the earlier matter remains vividly present. The mind that recites the Buddha should likewise be so. Or if the mindfulness is lost, draw it back again and again; in time it becomes a nature, and one recollects constantly, spontaneously. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: ‘If a being's mind recollects and recites the Buddha, then in the present and in the future he will surely see the Buddha, being not far from Buddhahood; without recourse to other expedient means, of himself his mind opens.’ Thus binding the mind, it naturally ever screens off
(blocks off)

all evil thoughts. Should one wish to do evil, because of recollecting the Buddha, the evil cannot be accomplished. Even when one follows evil and does evil deeds, the mind ever becomes soft and gentle, like a body that bears fragrance naturally putting off the stench. Again, when one perceives an evil thought faintly rising in the mind, one immediately recollects the Buddha; because of the Buddha's power, the evil thought is stilled of itself — like a person who meets with difficulty and seeks a powerful ally, and is surely delivered. Again, when one sees others suffering, with a mind of Buddha-recitation one feels compassion for them and wishes them to be free of suffering. If one is sentencing criminals
(passing judgment)
, because of recollecting the Buddha, a compassionate thought arises; though one follows the king's law, one should secretly
(that is, “silently”)

make a vow, saying: ‘I execute the king's law; this is not my original intention. May I be born in the Pure Land, and vow to rescue them all.’ Whatever circumstances one passes through, whether good or evil, because the mind recollects the Buddha, all are turned into vows by the mind. Therefore the King of Vows, Samantabhadra, says: ‘All evil that is done is not accomplished; if good deeds are done, all are brought to accord.’ This is that very meaning. Thus, with Buddha-recitation continuing unbroken in the mind, one can accomplish all the meritorious causes and virtues of the Pure Land.”
(The Two Gates of Resolving Doubts and Practicing Vows for Rebirth in the Pure Land)
Translation:

Whether in official duties or at home, passing through all manner of circumstances and affairs, though hurried, within the mind one never forgets the Buddha and recollects the Pure Land. It is like an ordinary person with a pressing matter fastened in mind: though he goes through conversation, coming and going, sitting and lying, and all manner of tasks, none of it hinders his secret recollection, and the matter remains vividly present before him.
The mind that recollects and recites the Buddha
should likewise be so. Or if the binding mindfulness is lost, one must draw it back again and again; in time it becomes a nature, and one recollects constantly, spontaneously. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra,
and in its

chapter on Mahasthamaprapta's Perfect Penetration through Buddha-Recitation, it says: ‘If a being's mind recollects and recites the Buddha, then in the present and in the future he will surely see the Buddha, being not far from Buddhahood; without recourse to other expedient means, of himself his mind opens.’ Thus binding the mind upon the Buddha, it naturally always screens off all evil thoughts. Should one wish to do evil, because of recollecting the Buddha, the evil cannot be accomplished. Even when one follows evil and does evil deeds, the mind ever becomes soft and gentle, like a body that bears fragrance naturally putting off the stench.

Again, whenever one perceives an evil thought faintly rising in the mind, one immediately recollects the Buddha; because of the Buddha's power, the evil thought is stilled of itself — like a person in difficulty who seeks help from a powerful ally, and is surely delivered.

Again, when one sees others suffering, with a mind of Buddha-recitation one feels compassion for them and wishes them to be free of suffering. If one is passing judgment, because of recollecting the Buddha, a compassionate thought arises; though one follows the king's law, one should silently make a vow, saying: ‘I execute the king's law; this is not my true intention. May you be born in the Pure Land; I vow to rescue you.’

In all circumstances one passes through, whether good or evil, because the mind is bound upon the Buddha, it is the true mind that is in command. Therefore the King of Vows, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, says: ‘All evil that is done is not accomplished; if good deeds are done, all are brought to accord.’ This is that very meaning. Thus, with Buddha-recitation continuing unbroken in the mind, one can accomplish all the meritorious causes and virtues of the Pure Land.

[I, in the causal stage, by a mind of Buddha-recitation, entered the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. Now, in this world, I draw in those who recite the Buddha, leading them home to the Pure Land.]

I, in the causal stage, by a mind of Buddha-recitation, entered the patience of the non-arising of dharmas and realized Perfect Penetration. Now I have come to this Sahā world, drawing in those who recite the Buddha, to lead them back to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[Causal stage] The counterpart of the “fruit stage”. “Stage” (dì) means position, rank. It refers to the stages of one's practice on the Buddha Way, that is, the stages between causal practice and the realization of the fruit; it is synonymous with “causal position”. Its meaning is threefold: First, relative to the Buddha's fruit position, all below Equal Enlightenment are the causal stage. Second, relative to the Bodhisattvas at and above the first ground, the stages of the Bodhisattvas before the ground are all the causal stage. Third, those who have already realized a position call those who have not yet realized it the causal stage.

[Patience of non-arising] That is, the patience of the non-arising of dharmas: true wisdom abiding in the principle that “all dharmas in origin have never arisen, and therefore do not cease”, no longer falling back. The Buddha says:
“All dharmas are all false and unreal.”
(The Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra) [Perfect Penetration] Pervading everything, fused and unobstructed. Here it refers to the principle of reality realized by the sublime wisdom of the sages.

Question: Of the Buddha-lands in the ten directions, there are very many Pure Lands. Why is “drawing in those who recite the Buddha, leading them home to the Pure Land” taken to mean drawing in those who recite the Buddha and leading them back to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss?

Answer: Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva is one of the Three Holy Ones of the West, and now, together with Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, assists Amitābha Buddha in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. When the Bodhisattva says “now, in this world, I draw in those who recite the Buddha, leading them home to the Pure Land”, it is of course that he draws in those who recite the Buddha and leads them back to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
[When the Buddha asked of Perfect Penetration, I made no other choice: gathering in all the six faculties, with pure mindfulness in unbroken succession, I attained samādhi — this is the foremost.]

The Buddha asked how I realized Perfect Penetration. I did not choose any other method of practice; rather, I gathered in the six faculties, not letting them grasp at the six sense objects, and so, with not a single thought arising (pure mindfulness in unbroken succession), I realized the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi. This method of practice is the first and most supreme.

[The six faculties] Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. [The six sense objects] The object of form, the object of sound, the object of smell, the object of taste, the object of touch, and the object of dharmas.
[Pure mindfulness] Pure mindfulness is no-mindfulness. When the Buddha-name continues unbroken, this is called “binding mindfulness”.
Master Hanshan says:
To be without thought is to have pure mindfulness.”
(The Dream-Wandering Collection: Reply to the Monk Haiyin of Huzhou)

[Unbroken succession of pure mindfulness] There are two levels in the unbroken succession of Buddha-recitation: first, the unbroken succession of binding mindfulness; second, the unbroken succession of pure mindfulness. When the thought of reciting the Buddha continues without any admixture of false thoughts, it is called “the unbroken succession of binding mindfulness”; when not a single thought arises (no-mindfulness), it is called “the unbroken succession of pure mindfulness”. On this, Master Hanshan taught:
“As for the four-syllable Buddha-name, when it continues unbroken, this is called binding mindfulness
, not pure mindfulness.
Right mindfulness is no-mindfulness.
To be without thought is to have pure mindfulness.
Only when right mindfulness is not darkened is there succession
(that is, the unbroken succession of pure mindfulness)
(The Dream-Wandering Collection: Reply to the Monk Haiyin of Huzhou; see its explanation in
An Exposition on Investigating Buddha-Recitation
Mr. Jiang Weinong, in his Lectures on the Diamond Sūtra, says:
“One should know that the aim of Buddha-recitation must return to no-mindfulness; this is to return to Suchness
(one's original nature)
, whereupon, without speaking of cutting off, it is cut off of itself
(that is, without speaking of cutting off the thought, the thought is cut off of itself)
, and, without expecting realization, it is realized of itself
(realization: thoroughly seeing one's original nature)
— how great is this expedient means!”
(See in detail
Reciting Yet Without Reciting
one article)

[Samādhi] That is, samādhi (sān-mèi). [Pure mindfulness in unbroken succession, one attains samādhi] When pure mindfulness continues in unbroken succession, one realizes the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi. In cultivating the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi there are three stages: first, all thoughts gathered into one (the mind single and unconfused in reciting the Buddha); second, not a single thought arising (pure mindfulness in unbroken succession); third, seeing the nature and making the mind clear. (See in detail
An Elucidation of Groping for the Elephant: Notes on the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi
) Therefore, the unbroken succession of pure mindfulness is the prelude to realizing the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi; hence it is said:
“With pure mindfulness in unbroken succession, one attains samādhi.”
Question: How does one accomplish “gathering in the six faculties, pure mindfulness in unbroken succession”?
Answer:
Investigating Buddha-Recitation
is the article that specifically explains how to accomplish “gathering in the six faculties, pure mindfulness in unbroken succession”.
